paper_title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026; Hubotter et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026) has emerged as promising paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), showing superiority over other post-training paradigms like Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (e.g., GRPO (Guo et al., 2025)). In OPSD, the same model serves as both student and teacher. The student generates rollout responses, while the teacher provides supervision with access to privileged references, such as reference solutions. Compared with RLVR, OPSD provides dense token-level learning signals beyond sparse outcome rewards. Compared with SFT, it trains on trajectories sampled by the student itself, mitigating the exposure bias (Bengio et al., 2015). Despite these advantages, recent studies (Kim et al., 2026; Kaur et al., 2026; Harne et al., 2026; Armandpour et al., 2026) reveal that OPSD can also suffer from degraded reasoning performance, which stems from the highly informative references exposed to the teacher. It may induce overly sharp teacher distributions, producing supervision that is poorly aligned with the students learning dynamics (e.g., suppressing uncertainty (Kim et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)). line of work (Tan & Hong, 2026; Han et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026c) has attempted to address this student-teacher mismatch through adaptive reference exposure. Rather than providing the teacher with the complete reference, it adjusts how much of the reference the teacher receives based on the students learning Correspondence to: Yifu Luo (yifu599@gmail.com) and Chuang Ma (ma.chuang.52h@st.kyoto-u.ac.jp).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: dynamics, such as the student-teacher gap. However, these methods adapt at the response level. Although reference exposure may vary across responses, it remains fixed across tokens within each response. In other words, all tokens in rollout are supervised by the same teacher. In this paper, we challenge this consensus by arguing: The adaptive teacher should operate at the token level, because every token requires its own dedicated teacher. teacher that provides useful guidance at one token may be less suitable at another, even within the same response. Rather than treating it with the same teacher, each token in the response merits consideration with its own preferred teacher. As illustrated in Figure 1, when different teachers are applied to the same response, they can provide similar learning signals for some tokens but disagree on the direction of supervision for others. This suggests that not only each response, but also each token, may have distinct teacher preferences. Figure 1: Token-level learning signals induced by different teachers for the same response. Teachers agree at some positions but provide opposing signals at others, motivating token-level teacher selection. Additional details on this visualization are provided in Section A. While some prior work (Wang et al., 2026c; Hao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Ke et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026a) has explored token selection for post-training (e.g., focusing solely on high-entropy tokens (Wang et al., 2026c)), how to validate our claim is challenging, and how to adaptively identify the preferred teacher for each token remains unexplored. To answer these, we conduct teacher-intervention pilot study (Section 4) to quantify the token-level teacher preference. As shown in Figure 2, we preserve student-generated prefix, allow candidate teacher to generate short continuation at selected token position, and then return control to the student to complete the response. The accuracy gain from this studentteacher-student relay over pure student generation serves as proxy for the teacher preference at that token position. large gain implies compatible teacher for that position, while small gain suggests the opposite. Interestingly, the results are simple, yet clear and compelling. First, teacher preferences differ across tokens, even within the same response. Second, at the token level, majority voting yields subset of reliable teachers, and the preferred teacher always exhibits large student-teacher KL distance. The first finding validates our claim, and the second finding motivates practical rule for token-level teacher selection. Based on these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTAOPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. As shown in Figure 3, MTA-OPSD constructs multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, by varying the truncation strategy and exposure ratio of the privileged reference. During training, rather than using fixed teacher for all tokens in the same response, each token adaptively selects its own teacher from the multi-teacher pool based on its preference, through majority voting followed by KL-based selection. Our token-level adaptive OPSD design is simple yet effective, precisely addressing the student-teacher mismatch. By assigning each token its preferred teacher, MTA-OPSD provides more balanced learning signal rather than an overly sharp, rigid teacher distribution from single teacher. We evaluate MTA-OPSD on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family (Yang et al., 2025), and it consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to +5.9 over the base model. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We quantify the teacher preference across tokens via teacher-intervention pilot study, validating that preferred teachers can differ from token to token within the same response. We further reveal that the token-level preferred teacher can be identified through majority voting and KL-based selection. We propose MTA-OPSD, the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. By constructing multi-teacher pool as the supervision source, our approach enables each token to adap-

sections.content: tively select its preferred teacher under the guidance of majority voting and KL divergence, effectively addressing the student-teacher mismatch. We conduct extensive experiments across various models on mathematical reasoning tasks, demonstrating that our approach achieves superior reasoning performance compared to existing OPSD methods. Furthermore, we empirically analyze comprehensive ablation studies, paving the way for future advances in this field.

sections.title: 2.1 ON-POLICY DISTILLATION AND ON-POLICY SELF-DISTILLATION
sections.content: Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) transfers knowledge from large teacher model to student model by training on the teachers soft output distributions. Early approaches (Kim & Rush, 2016; Jiao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) leveraged it to sequence-level distillation, establishing the dominant off-policy distillation approaches. (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu & Lab, 2025; Yang et al., 2026b) extended it to On-policy Distillation (OPD), addressing the exposure bias (Bengio et al., 2015) mismatch by shifting the training distribution to the students own generations. Despite the rapid progress of OPD, the paradigm relies on separate, typically stronger teacher model, which may be unavailable or expensive to maintain. To address this challenge, OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026; Hubotter et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a) removes this requirement by instantiating the teacher and student from the same model. Under this setting, the teacher and student share the same model, but the teacher is granted access to privileged reference unavailable to the student. However, recent studies (Kim et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Kaur et al., 2026; Harne et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026) reveal persistent mismatch in OPSD. In particular, highly informative reference can induce an overly sharp teacher distribution and create mismatch between the teachers supervision and the students learning dynamics. These observations motivate the line of research for adaptive OPSD methods. 2.2 ADAPTIVE ON-POLICY SELF-DISTILLATION Adaptive OPSD seeks to align the teacher supervision with the students learning dynamics. Rather than exposing the complete privileged reference, existing methods (Tan & Hong, 2026; Han et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026c) control its content or exposure ratio using mechanisms such as learned reference-exposure schedules. By varying the amount of privileged references available to the teacher, these methods aim to avoid overly sharp supervision while retaining the benefits of dense learning signals. However, these methods adapt at the response level, where all tokens in the response share the same teacher and the same privileged reference. In contrast, we identify that each token needs its own teacher as tokens have distinct teacher preferences (Section 4), and further propose our token-level multi-teacher adaptive OPSD method.

sections.title: 4 PILOT STUDY: TOKEN MATTERS
sections.content: Before diving into detailed design, critical question must first be answered: Given ci = (y<i, x), how can we determine if one teacher pT (ci) is more suitable than another? direct approach would be to train on every token separately with specific teachers, covering enough token-teacher combinations. However, it is obviously not practical. We instead answer this question from another view. Motivated by (Xu et al., 2025; 2026a), we estimate teacher suitability through teacher intervention. Specifically, given prompt and students response = {y1, y2, , yL}, we select token position 1 < < and preserve the student-generated prefix before that position. Starting from position i, candidate teacher takes over the generation process and produces short subsequence: Figure 2: Illustration of the teacher-intervention pilot study. z1:i1 = y1:i1 = pθ(x) zt:t+k = pT (y<i, x) = pθ(ci, r), where denotes the teacher-intervention length. After this intervention, control is returned to the student, which completes the remainder of the response: (4) zi+k+1:L = pθ(z<i+k+1, x). (5) Thus, we obtain student-teacher-student relay response = {z1, z2, , zL}. We compare its accuracy with the pure student response, which serves as proxy for the candidate teacher preference at the selected token position. larger gain indicates more suitable teacher, whereas smaller gain indicates the opposite. The main purpose of this pilot study is that, by varying both the intervention token position and the candidate teacher, this study separates variation along the token and teacher axes. This allows us to examine whether teacher preferences change across token positions and to identify their patterns. Interestingly, the pattern is simple but clear. We next describe the experimental setup and then present our findings, as highlighted in Section 4.2. 4.1 SETUP Our study varies two principal factors: tokens at which the intervention begins, and teachers which are used for the intervention.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: For the token axis, we consider both regular-spaced and statistic-extreme token positions. For the former, we select tokens located at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the original student rollout. For the latter, we select tokens associated with the highest and lowest student entropy, and the largest and smallest student-teacher KL distance 0. In total, we select 7 intervention positions from each rollout. For the teacher axis, we vary both the reference-truncation strategy1 and the reference-exposure ratio. We consider prefix, suffix, and random-span for truncation strategy, each with exposure ratios of 0.5 and 0.75, together with full-reference teacher. This produces 7 candidate teachers. We evaluate intervention lengths across = 64, 128, and 256. We sample 64 prompts of at least medium difficulty2 from DeepMath-103k (He et al., 2026). We conduct the study using Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B as student models. To reduce sampling variance, for every experimental configuration, we sample 2 teacher continuations and then 2 student relays following each continuation. In total, 64 7 7 3 2 2 2 = 75264 generations are evaluated.

sections.title: 5 METHOD
sections.content: Based on the findings in Section 4.2, we propose Multi-Teacher Adaptive OPSD (MTA-OPSD), simple yet effective framework for token-level adaptive OPSD. As illustrated in Figure 3, rather than using single teacher, MTA-OPSD constructs multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers conditioned on different variants of the privileged reference. Through majority voting followed by KL-based selection, it assigns each token its preferred teacher. This ensures that different tokens within the same response receive supervision from their respective teachers. 5.1 MULTI-TEACHER POOL To support token-level adaptive teacher selection, we construct multi-teacher pool , consisting of all candidate teachers available for each token: = {pT1 , pT2, , pTK }, (7) where is the number of candidate teachers and pTk denotes the k-th teacher. All teachers share the same model pθ with the student. They differ from each other only in the privileged references on which they are conditioned: = {r1, r2, , rK}, which leads to the next-token distribution of each teacher as: pTk = pθ( x, rk). (8) (9) Each rk differs from each other by its truncation way and exposure ratio of the full reference. An example of our multi-teacher pool is provided in Section F. While the multi-teacher pool supplies diverse set of supervision signals, it does not determine which teacher should supervise each token. Guided by the pilot study in Section 4, MTA-OPSD performs token-level adaptive teacher assignment in two steps: (1) majority voting identifies reliable subset of teachers, and (2) KL-based selection chooses the preferred teacher from that subset. 5.2 MAJORITY VOTING As shown in Section 4.2, majority voting provides reliable teacher subset by identifying the direction of the advantage signals. We therefore use majority voting as the first step of teacher selection. Specifically, for token yi in the student response, the multi-teacher pool produces the following set of its teacher token distributions: PM (ci) = {pT1 ( ci), pT2( ci), , pTK ( ci)} = {pθ( ci, r1), pθ( ci, r2), , pθ( ci, rK)} . sections.title: 5.4 DISCUSSION
sections.content: The mechanism of our method can be understood as decoupling the reliability of the supervision direction from the informativeness of the supervision signal. Majority voting first determines whether the teacher pool collectively supports or opposes the student-generated token yi, KL-based selection then identifies the most informative teacher aligned with that direction. This ordering is crucial: KL distance is not used as standalone measure of teacher quality, but only after directional consensus has filtered out potentially unreliable teachers. Specifically, when VM (ci) = 1, the majority teachers in Mmaj(ci) assign higher probability to yi than the student itself, and selecting the teacher with the largest KL therefore reinforces the students current choice. Meanwhile, the selected teacher can also provide substantially different overall probability distribution. Consequently, the supervision can strengthen the sampled token without being limited to simply imitating it, thereby retaining informative probabilities for other plausible predictions and potentially reducing overfitting to the students current trajectory. When VM (ci) = 1, the majority teachers assign lower probability to yi, and the sampled token is collectively regarded as less preferred choice. In this case, teacher with small KL distance may only weakly downweight this token or remain too close to the student distribution. In contrast, the farthest teacher is more likely to redistribute probability mass toward different candidate tokens, providing stronger corrective signal together with more distinct alternative prediction directions. Such supervision may therefore help the student move away from potentially erroneous local choice rather than merely making marginal adjustment to it.

sections.title: 6 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 6.1 EXPERIMENT SETUP Additional experiment setup details are provided in Section C. Models and Datasets. We evaluate models from the Qwen3 family (Yang et al., 2025) at three scales: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B, all with thinking mode enabled during both training and validation. We conduct experiments across mathematical reasoning tasks. The training data is drawn from DeepMath-103K (He et al., 2026), and we evaluate on AMC23 (MAA, 2023), AIME24 (Zhang & Math-AI, 2024), and AIME25 (Zhang & Math-AI, 2025). Baselines. We compare our method against two fixed-teacher OPSD methods and one adaptive OPSD method: (1) OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026), which performs dense-logit distillation using forward KL with token-wise pointwise KL clipping; (2) SDPO (Hubotter et al., 2026), which performs dense-logit distillation using JensenShannon divergence; and (3) Paint (Tan & Hong, 2026), which adaptively determines the reference-exposure ratio according to the student-teacher gap. Implementation Details. All baselines and our method use dataset-provided ground-truth reference solutions as the privileged information, and all contexts include both the reasoning trace and the final answer. We use identical training and evaluation settings across all methods, with maximum generation lengths of 4096 tokens during training and 38912 tokens during validation. The multi-teacher pool contains seven teacher configurations: {full reference, prefix-0.5, prefix-0.75, suffix-0.5, suffix-0.75, random-span-0.5, random-span-0.75}4. We train each method for 300 steps, evaluate checkpoints every 50 steps on the test set, and report its best Avg@12 results. 6.2 MAIN RESULTS Table 5 presents comprehensive reasoning performance comparison between existing OPSD methods and our approach. For average performance, MTA-OPSD achieves the highest average performance at every model scale, yielding an average improvement of +5.9 for Qwen3-1.7B, +1.5 for Qwen3-4B, and +2.8 for Qwen3-8B, over the base model. These results outperform existing OPSD methods. As shown in Table 7, MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms both alternatives on every benchmark. These show that the gains do not arise solely from multiple teachers; selecting suitable teacher for each token is critical to using the teacher pool effectively. Teacher-Assignment Dynamics. We also investigate how frequently each teacher is selected throughout training. The assignments are distributed relatively evenly across the teacher pool, indicating that the selection mechanism does not collapse to single dominant teacher. We also observe that, under the same truncation strategy, higher reference-exposure ratio does not necessarily produce larger student-teacher KL distance, as discussed in Section E. This observation further suggests that existing adaptive methods of adjusting reference exposure alone cannot determine teacher suitability. Effect of Majority Voting and KL-Based Selection. MTA-OPSD selects teacher in two steps: majority voting and KL-based selection. Table 8 presents the contribution of each step, where the second row is our default setting. MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms all variants, further validating the effectiveness of our design: majority voting first identifies reliable teacher subset, and KL-based selection chooses teacher from that subset.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present MTA-OPSD, the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. teacher-intervention study shows that teacher preferences vary across tokens and motivates our two-step token-level adaptive teacher selection strategy: majority voting with KL-based selection. Future work may explore selfevolving teacher pools and more stable multi-teacher training.

sections.title: B ADDITIONAL MAJORITY VOTING DETAILS
sections.content: As discussed in Section 5.2, tie may occur when the multi-teacher pool contains an even number of teachers, with equal numbers of positive and negative votes. In this case, we break the tie according to the magnitudes of the corresponding advantage signals. Specifically, the majority direction is defined as VM (ci) = sgn sgn (cid:32) (cid:88) k=1 (cid:32) (cid:88) k=1 (cid:33) vTk (ci) , if (cid:33) (cid:88) k=1 vTk (ci) = 0, (17) aTk (yi ci) , otherwise. Thus, when the numbers of positive and negative votes are equal, we select the group with the larger total absolute advantage. The majority teacher subset is then still constructed using Equation (14). This tie-breaking rule retains the direction supported by the stronger aggregate teacher signal.

sections.title: C ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENT SETTINGS
sections.content: All experiments are conducted on 4 H200 GPUs. We use learning rate of 1 106. All methods are implemented on top of the veRL (Sheng et al., 2025) PPO trainer with FSDP2 actor sharding and vLLM rollouts. All runs use full-parameter training (no LoRA (Hu et al., 2021)). The global batch size is 32. Following (Zhao et al., 2026), we restrict the token-level distillation objective to the top-100 entries of the teacher distribution. Note that following (Pan et al., 2026), we use training problems at difficulty levels 57 for Qwen31.7B, 68 for Qwen3-4B, and levels 710 for Qwen3-8B.
